chapter.name: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life

questions.q: Which of these is a part of the cryosphere?
questions.a: Snow in Ladakh: the cryosphere is water in solid form, such as ice and snow.

questions.q:
Match column I with column II.
Column I: 1. Thar desert  2. Groundwater  3. Polar ice caps  4. Mangroves
Column II: (p) biosphere  (q) geosphere  (r) cryosphere  (s) hydrosphere
questions.a: 1-q, 2-s, 3-r, 4-p: the Thar desert is a landform of the geosphere, groundwater is liquid water of the hydrosphere, polar ice caps are solid water of the cryosphere, and mangroves are living organisms of the biosphere.

questions.q: (a) Name the sphere of the Earth that is the air surrounding the Earth that we breathe. (b) Name the sphere made up of all living organisms and their habitats, and give one example of it from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The atmosphere. (b) The biosphere; for example mangroves, forests, farms, ocean plankton or coral reefs.
s: (a) atmosphere
(b) biosphere, with one example such as mangroves, forests, farms, plankton or coral reefs

questions.q: Name the sphere to which each of these belongs, and give a reason in each case: (a) ocean plankton (b) Himalayan glaciers (c) the Earth's interior.
questions.a: (a) Biosphere: plankton are living organisms. (b) Cryosphere: glaciers are water in solid form (ice). (c) Geosphere: the geosphere includes solid rocks, soil, landforms and the Earth's interior.
s: (a) biosphere, because plankton are living organisms
(b) cryosphere, because glaciers are solid water (ice)
(c) geosphere, which includes the Earth's interior

questions.q: According to the chapter, a rise in atmospheric temperature can finally lead to the loss of habitats along a coast. In which order are the spheres disturbed along this chain?
o: Atmosphere, then cryosphere, then hydrosphere, then biosphere
Cryosphere, then atmosphere, then biosphere, then hydrosphere
Hydrosphere, then cryosphere, then atmosphere, then biosphere
Atmosphere, then biosphere, then hydrosphere, then cryosphere
questions.a: Atmosphere, then cryosphere, then hydrosphere, then biosphere: warmer air speeds up the melting of glaciers and polar ice, the meltwater floods low-lying land and raises sea levels, and this causes habitat loss for living things.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A change in the cryosphere of a mountain region can affect the biosphere around it.
Reason (R): Glaciers and snow are water in solid form.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: R only says what the cryosphere is made of. A is explained by the link between spheres: snow and ice melt into lakes and rivers (hydrosphere), and that water supports the grass, crops and animals (biosphere), so less snow means less water for living things.

questions.q: Kavya says, 'Each of the Earth's spheres can be studied on its own, because a change in one sphere stays inside that sphere.' Using the chapter's example of the Arabian Sea becoming warmer, show in three steps that she is wrong.
questions.a: She is wrong. Step 1: warmer Arabian Sea water (hydrosphere) leads to more evaporation, adding moisture to the air (atmosphere). Step 2: this causes fluctuations in the southwest monsoon, so rainfall over India becomes variable. Step 3: some regions get floods and others are left in drought, which disrupts the hydrosphere and the life and farming on land; so a change in one sphere passes into others.
s: warmer sea water causes more evaporation into the atmosphere
this causes fluctuations in the southwest monsoon and variable rainfall
floods in some regions and drought in others: the change spreads to other spheres, so Kavya is wrong

questions.q: A glacier feeds a river that flows past a village in Uttarakhand. Survey records show that over the last 20 years the front of the glacier has moved back by 300 m. Elders say winter snowfall has also become lighter. In the last five summers the river has flooded the low-lying wheat fields of the village three times, and older farmers worry about what will happen when the glacier becomes much smaller. (a) Name the sphere to which the glacier, the river and the wheat crop each belong. (b) Find the average distance the glacier front moved back each year. (c) Explain the chain of events from a rise in air temperature to the flooded fields. (d) Elders say winter snowfall has become lighter. Using the chapter, predict what will happen in the long run to the river's summer water and the village's crops and grazing grass once the glacier is much smaller, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Glacier: cryosphere; river: hydrosphere; wheat crop: biosphere. (b) 300 m / 20 years = 15 m per year. (c) A rise in atmospheric temperature speeds up the melting of the glacier, so more meltwater enters the river in summer; the river overflows and floods the low-lying fields, disturbing the crops. (d) With lighter snowfall and a smaller glacier, less snow and ice is stored, so less meltwater reaches the river in summer. The river will carry less water, leaving less water to support the growth of crops and grass; the floods now are only short-term, and a shortage will follow.
s: (a) cryosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere
(b) 300 / 20 = 15 m per year
(c) warmer air speeds up melting, more meltwater in the river, low-lying fields flood
(d) less snow and ice stored, so less summer water in the river and less water for crops and grass, with the link explained

questions.q: What is the amount of the Sun's radiation that reaches the Earth's surface called?
questions.a: Insolation: it is the amount of the Sun's radiation reaching the Earth's surface, while the solar constant is measured at the top of the atmosphere.

questions.q: A solar cooker has a reflector of area 0.5 m2 facing the Sun. The insolation is 1 kWm-2 (1000 J s-1 m-2). How much solar energy falls on the reflector in 10 minutes?

Assertion (A): UV rays are used in water purifiers.
Reason (R): UV rays are useful in killing germs.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: water purifiers use UV rays because UV rays kill germs in the water.

questions.q: (a) Name the three regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in which about 99 per cent of the Sun's energy reaching the Earth falls. (b) Name the two high-energy radiations that are mostly filtered out by the Earth's upper atmosphere.
questions.a: (a) Ultraviolet (UV), visible and infrared (IR). (b) Gamma rays and X-rays.
s: (a) ultraviolet, visible and infrared
(b) gamma rays and X-rays

questions.q: Answer these questions on solar energy. (a) Give the value of the solar constant in kWm-2 and in J s-1 m-2. (b) What is insolation? (c) About how much is the greatest insolation at the Earth's surface under a clear sky? (d) Under that insolation, how much solar energy falls on a 1.5 m2 panel in 20 minutes? (e) Give one reason why the insolation at the surface is lower than the solar constant.
questions.a: (a) About 1.4 kWm-2, or about 1400 J s-1 m-2. (b) The amount of the Sun's radiation that reaches the Earth's surface. (c) About 1 kWm-2. (d) E = 1000 × 1.5 × 1200 = 1800000 J = 1.8 × 10^6 J. (e) Some of the energy is absorbed and scattered by gases, clouds and dust particles in the atmosphere before it reaches the surface.
s: (b) the Sun's radiation reaching the Earth's surface
(c) about 1 kWm-2
(e) gases, clouds and dust absorb and scatter some energy

questions.q: The solar constant is about 1.4 kWm-2. How much solar energy reaches 1 m2 at the top of the atmosphere, held perpendicular to the Sun's rays, in one minute?
questions.a: 8.4 × 10^4 J: 1.4 kWm-2 = 1400 J s-1 m-2, so in 60 s one square metre receives 1400 × 60 = 84000 J.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Electromagnetic waves from the Sun travel through a vacuum at the speed of light.
II. Gamma rays and X-rays are low-frequency, long-wavelength radiations.
III. Visible light from the Sun provides the energy for photosynthesis.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: gamma rays and X-rays are high-frequency, short-wavelength radiations with very high energy.

questions.q: Take the solar constant as 1400 J s-1 m-2 and the clear-sky insolation at the surface as 1000 J s-1 m-2. (a) Find the energy received by 1 m2 in 10 minutes at the top of the atmosphere. (b) Find the energy received by 1 m2 at the surface in the same time, and the difference. (c) Explain where the missing energy goes.
questions.a: (a) 1400 × 600 = 840000 J = 8.4 × 10^5 J. (b) 1000 × 600 = 600000 J = 6.0 × 10^5 J; difference = 240000 J = 2.4 × 10^5 J. (c) On the way down, part of the energy is absorbed and scattered by gases, clouds and dust particles in the atmosphere, so less reaches the surface.
s: (a) 8.4 × 10^5 J at the top
(b) 6.0 × 10^5 J at the surface, difference 2.4 × 10^5 J
(c) absorbed and scattered by gases, clouds and dust

questions.q: The flat roof of a shop in Nagpur has a dark sheet of area 2 m2. On a clear day it receives an insolation of 0.9 kWm-2 for 2 hours. The chapter says that 3.6 × 10^6 J is about one unit of household electricity and is about the energy needed to melt 5 kg of ice and heat the water to 100 °C. (a) Find the solar energy falling on the sheet. (b) Express this in units of electricity. (c) Using the chapter's comparison, about how many kilograms of ice could this energy melt and heat to 100 °C? (d) Find the energy the same area would receive in the same time at the top of the atmosphere, and explain why the two answers differ.
questions.a: (a) E = 900 × 2 × 7200 = 12960000 J = 1.296 × 10^7 J. (b) 1.296 × 10^7 / 3.6 × 10^6 = 3.6 units. (c) 3.6 × 5 kg = 18 kg. (d) At the top of the atmosphere: 1400 × 2 × 7200 = 2.016 × 10^7 J. It is more because, before reaching the roof, part of the Sun's energy is absorbed and scattered by gases, clouds and dust in the atmosphere.
s: (b) 3.6 units
(c) about 18 kg of ice
(d) 2.016 × 10^7 J at the top; less at the surface because the atmosphere absorbs and scatters some energy

questions.q: What is the fraction of solar radiation reflected by a surface called?
questions.a: Albedo: it is the fraction of solar radiation that a surface reflects; the word comes from Latin for whiteness.

questions.q: A patch of ice has an albedo of 0.6. Out of 500 J of sunlight falling on it, how much energy does it absorb?
questions.a: 200 J: an albedo of 0.6 means 0.6 × 500 = 300 J is reflected, so 500 - 300 = 200 J is absorbed.

questions.q: True or False: 'Equatorial regions stay warm all year because the Sun's rays there are spread over a larger area.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Because the Earth is spherical, the Sun's radiation falling on the equatorial region is concentrated over a smaller area; it is near the poles that it is spread over a larger area.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: at the equator the rays are concentrated over a smaller area; near the poles they spread over a larger area

questions.q: (a) Snow has an albedo of 0.80-0.90, ice 0.50-0.70 and crushed rock 0.25-0.30. Which of the three reflects the largest share of sunlight? (b) Why do dark coloured roads heat up quickly in the sun? (c) Why do people feel hot inside a concrete house at night in summer?
questions.a: (a) Snow (albedo 0.80-0.90). (b) Dark surfaces have a low albedo: they reflect less and absorb more sunlight. (c) The concrete absorbs heat during the day and re-radiates it during the night.
s: (a) snow, albedo 0.80-0.90
(b) dark surfaces absorb more and reflect less sunlight
(c) concrete re-radiates at night the heat it absorbed by day

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Polar regions experience much colder conditions than equatorial regions.
Reason (R): Because the Earth is spherical, the Sun's radiation near the poles is spread over a larger area than at the equator.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the Sun's rays strike different latitudes at different angles; at the equator the radiation is concentrated over a smaller area, near the poles it is spread over a larger area, so each part of the polar surface gets less energy and stays colder.

questions.q: A light meter shows that a patch of ice reflects 390 J of every 600 J of sunlight falling on it, and a patch of crushed rock reflects 165 J of every 600 J. (a) Find the albedo of each surface. (b) Which surface will heat up more quickly, and why?
questions.a: (a) Albedo is the fraction reflected: ice 390 / 600 = 0.65; crushed rock 165 / 600 = 0.275. (b) The crushed rock: low albedo surfaces reflect less and absorb more light, so they heat up more quickly.
s: (a) ice 0.65, crushed rock 0.275
(b) crushed rock, because its lower albedo means it reflects less and absorbs more

questions.q: In a large city the use of air conditioners keeps rising on summer nights. Which explanation from the chapter fits best?
o: Steel, concrete, brick and asphalt absorb solar radiation, retain heat and re-radiate it, keeping the city warmer than nearby rural areas
The city lies closer to the equator than the nearby villages, so it gets more sunlight
The trees in the city transpire more water than the trees in the villages
Cities have more trees than villages, so they transpire more and trap heat
questions.a: The built materials of a city (steel, concrete, brick, asphalt) absorb and retain heat and re-radiate it; this urban heat island effect keeps the city warmer, which increases the energy demand for air conditioning.

questions.q: As a model, a beam of sunlight carrying 1200 J every second falls on the Earth at two places. At the equator it strikes nearly straight down and is spread over 1 m2 of crushed rock (albedo 0.3). Near a pole it strikes at a low angle and is spread over 3 m2 of snow (albedo 0.85). (a) Find the energy reaching each square metre per second at each place. (b) Find the energy absorbed per square metre per second at the equator. (c) Find the energy absorbed per square metre per second near the pole. (d) How many times more energy does each square metre absorb at the equator? (e) Name the two causes of uneven heating that this model combines.
questions.a: (a) Equator: 1200 / 1 = 1200 J per m2 per second; pole: 1200 / 3 = 400 J per m2 per second. (b) (1 - 0.3) × 1200 = 840 J. (c) (1 - 0.85) × 400 = 60 J. (d) 840 / 60 = 14 times. (e) Latitude and the Earth's shape (the rays are concentrated over a smaller area at the equator and spread over a larger area near the poles), and albedo (snow reflects far more sunlight than rock).
s: (a) 1200 J per m2 at the equator, 400 J per m2 near the pole
(b) 840 J absorbed at the equator
(c) 60 J absorbed near the pole
(d) 14 times
(e) latitude and Earth's shape, and albedo

questions.q: At a Himalayan research station, a 50 m2 patch of ground near the hut is covered with snow (albedo 0.85) in early spring. By late spring the snow has melted and bare crushed rock (albedo 0.28) is exposed. On both days the sunlight reaching the ground is 600 J per second per m2. (a) What does an albedo of 0.85 tell you about the snow? (b) Find the energy reflected per square metre per second by the snow and by the rock. (c) Hence find how much more energy the whole 50 m2 patch keeps every second once it is bare rock. (d) A scientist says that once snow starts melting, the ground around it tends to warm even faster. Do the figures support her? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The snow reflects 85% of the sunlight falling on it and absorbs only 15%. (b) Snow: 0.85 × 600 = 510 J; rock: 0.28 × 600 = 168 J per m2 per second. (c) Each square metre reflects 510 - 168 = 342 J less and so keeps 342 J more every second; for 50 m2 this is 342 × 50 = 17100 J every second. (d) Yes. Once the snow (cryosphere) melts, the exposed low-albedo rock (geosphere) reflects far less and keeps much more of the sunlight, so it heats faster; this can warm the surroundings and melt more of the nearby snow.
s: (a) 85% reflected, 15% absorbed
(b) snow 510 J, rock 168 J per m2 per second
(c) 342 J per m2 more, 17100 J per second for 50 m2
(d) yes: bare rock reflects less and keeps more energy, so exposed ground warms faster and melts more snow

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer found?
questions.a: Stratosphere: the ozone layer lies in the stratosphere (12-50 km), where ozone absorbs UV rays.

questions.q: The air at the ground is at 25 °C. Using the chapter's rate of fall of temperature in the troposphere (about 6.5 °C per km), what is the temperature of the air 2 km above the ground?
questions.a: 12 °C: the temperature falls by 6.5 × 2 = 13 °C, so 25 - 13 = 12 °C.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the atmosphere.
I. The atmosphere is held in place by the force of the Earth's gravity.
II. It consists mainly of nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%).
III. Nearly all weather phenomena take place in the stratosphere.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: nearly all weather phenomena take place in the troposphere.

questions.q: (a) Name any two greenhouse gases mentioned in the chapter. (b) What do these gases absorb that keeps the Earth warm?
questions.a: (a) Any two of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and water vapour. (b) The heat re-radiated by the Earth's surface in the infrared region, which would otherwise escape into space.
s: (a) two of carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour
(b) the infrared heat re-radiated from the Earth's surface

questions.q: On a summer afternoon the air at the ground in Bhopal is at 34 °C. Taking the fall of temperature in the troposphere as 6.5 °C per km, find the air temperature at heights of (a) 1 km, (b) 2 km and (c) 4 km above the ground. (d) In which layer of the atmosphere do all three heights lie?
questions.a: (a) 34 - 6.5 = 27.5 °C. (b) 34 - 13 = 21 °C. (c) 34 - 26 = 8 °C. (d) The troposphere, which extends to an average height of about 12 km.
s: (a) 27.5 °C at 1 km
(b) 21 °C at 2 km
(c) 8 °C at 4 km
(d) troposphere (0-12 km)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Nearly all weather phenomena, such as storms and clouds, take place in the troposphere.
Reason (R): In the stratosphere the temperature falls with height, which stops the air from mixing.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: in the stratosphere the temperature rises with height, because ozone absorbs UV rays; this rise calms the layer by preventing vertical mixing of air, which keeps weather confined to the troposphere.

questions.q: Priya says, 'Ozone absorbs UV rays, so the ozone hole over Antarctica means less UV now reaches the ground there.' Is she right? Explain, and name what caused the hole and what is helping it recover.
questions.a: No. Where the ozone layer becomes thinner it absorbs less UV, so more harmful UV radiation reaches the ground and can harm living organisms. The hole was caused by human-made CFCs used in refrigerators and aerosols. The Montreal Protocol reduced the use of CFCs, and the ozone layer is now slowly recovering.
s: Verdict: no, a thinner ozone layer lets more UV reach the ground
CFCs from refrigerators and aerosols caused the ozone hole
The Montreal Protocol cut CFC use and the layer is slowly recovering

questions.q: True or False: 'Outer space begins where the stratosphere ends, about 50 km above the Earth.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Above the stratosphere lie the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere; outer space is taken to begin at about 100 km above the Earth.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere lie above the stratosphere; outer space begins at about 100 km

questions.q: A weather balloon is released at Chennai, where the air at the ground is at 31 °C, and it rises steadily. Take the troposphere as 0-12 km and the fall of temperature in it as 6.5 °C per km. (a) Find the air temperature at 6 km. (b) At about what height will the air temperature be 0 °C? (c) At 20 km, in which layer is the balloon, and does the temperature there rise or fall with height? Why? (d) Why are storms and clouds not formed around the balloon at 20 km? (e) How much higher must the balloon go from 20 km to reach the start of outer space?
questions.a: (a) 31 - 6.5 × 6 = 31 - 39 = -8 °C. (b) 31 / 6.5 ≈ 4.8 km. (c) The stratosphere (12-50 km); the temperature rises with height because ozone there absorbs UV rays and heats the air. (d) Because temperature rises with height in the stratosphere, there is little vertical mixing of air, which calms the layer and keeps weather confined to the troposphere. (e) Outer space begins at about 100 km, so about 100 - 20 = 80 km more.
s: (a) -8 °C at 6 km
(b) about 4.8 km
(c) stratosphere; temperature rises because ozone absorbs UV
(d) little vertical mixing in the stratosphere keeps weather in the troposphere
(e) about 80 km more

questions.q: After sunset in a Himalayan valley near Shimla, cool air flows down the slopes into the valley. What is this wind called?
questions.a: Mountain breeze: after sunset the slopes cool faster, and the cooler, denser air over them flows down into the valley.

questions.q:
Match column I with column II.
Column I: 1. Valley breeze  2. Mountain breeze  3. Gyre  4. Gulf Stream
Column II: (p) a large circular pattern of moving ocean water  (q) cool air moving up the slopes by day to replace rising warm air  (r) a strong current carrying warm water from the southern part of the North American east coast across the Atlantic  (s) cool, dense air flowing down the slopes into the valley at night
questions.a: 1-q, 2-s, 3-p, 4-r: the valley breeze blows up the slopes by day, the mountain breeze flows down into the valley at night, a gyre is a large circular pattern of ocean currents, and the Gulf Stream carries warm water from the southern part of the North American east coast across the Atlantic.

questions.q: True or False: 'In the Northern Hemisphere, planetary winds are deflected towards the right.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The rotation of the Earth on its axis deflects the winds from straight paths: towards the right in the Northern Hemisphere and towards the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the Earth's rotation deflects winds, to the right in the Northern Hemisphere (left in the Southern)

questions.q: (a) What are ocean currents? (b) How do strong planetary winds set the surface water of the oceans moving? (c) In which direction do gyres rotate in the Northern Hemisphere and in the Southern Hemisphere?
questions.a: (a) Ocean currents are the continuous movement of large masses of ocean water. (b) The winds drag the surface water because of friction, setting surface currents in motion. (c) Clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counter-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
s: (a) continuous movement of large masses of ocean water
(b) winds drag the surface water by friction
(c) clockwise in the Northern, counter-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere

questions.q: Students on an ocean research ship in the North Atlantic take two water samples at the same spot. Sample A, from the surface, is at 26 °C and has lower salinity. Sample B, from a deep level, is at 4 °C and has higher salinity. The ship's log notes that warm water from near the equator flows over the surface towards the north-west of Europe. (a) Which sample is denser? (b) Which sample belongs to water that is moving towards the poles? (c) In which direction do gyres rotate in this hemisphere? (d) Name the warm current, an extension of the Gulf Stream, that keeps many ports of north-western Europe ice-free in winter.
questions.a: (a) Sample B: colder water with higher salinity is denser and sinks to deeper levels. (b) Sample A: warm equatorial water travels over the surface towards the poles, while colder, denser water flows back towards the equator at depth. (c) Clockwise, since the North Atlantic is in the Northern Hemisphere. (d) The North Atlantic Drift.
s: (a) Sample B, colder and saltier, is denser
(b) Sample A, warm surface water moving poleward
(c) clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere
(d) the North Atlantic Drift

questions.q: Near a polar region, a mass of surface sea water becomes colder and its salinity rises. What is it most likely to do next?
o: Become denser, sink and flow towards the equator at deeper levels
Stay at the surface and flow towards the equator
Become denser, sink and flow further towards the pole at deeper levels
Become less dense, rise and flow towards the pole at the surface
questions.a: It becomes denser, sinks and flows towards the equator at deeper levels: both colder water and higher salinity water are denser and sink, and colder, denser waters slowly flow back towards the equator through deeper ocean levels.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Gyres in the Southern Hemisphere rotate counter-clockwise.
Reason (R): Continents block and redirect ocean currents.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the gyres form and turn counter-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere because of the Earth's rotation; continents only further modify the paths of currents.

questions.q: Warm air rises over the equator. Explain why this air sinks around 30° North and South, and name the belt that forms there.
questions.a: The rising air moves towards the poles at higher altitudes; as it cools it becomes denser and sinks around 30° North and South. This forms the sub-tropical high pressure belts.
s: the air moves poleward at height, cools and becomes denser, so it sinks
sub-tropical high pressure belt

questions.q: Four weather stations lie along one line of longitude: W at the equator, X at 30°N, Y at 60°N and Z at 90°N. (a) Name the pressure belt at each station. (b) At which of these stations does air mainly rise, and at which does it mainly sink? (c) Along the surface between X and W, in which direction would the air flow if the Earth did not rotate? (d) How does the Earth's rotation change the path of this surface wind? (e) Explain why air flows along the surface from Z towards Y.
questions.a: (a) W: equatorial low; X: sub-tropical high; Y: sub-polar low; Z: polar high. (b) Air rises at W and Y (low pressure belts) and sinks at X and Z (high pressure belts). (c) From X towards W, that is from the sub-tropical high towards the equatorial low (towards the equator). (d) The rotation deflects it from a straight path to the right (in the Northern Hemisphere), so it follows a curved path instead of moving directly from high to low pressure. (e) At Z the very low temperature makes the air cold and dense, so it sinks and forms high pressure; air flows from this polar high towards the sub-polar low at Y, completing another circulation cycle.
s: (a) W equatorial low, X sub-tropical high, Y sub-polar low, Z polar high
(b) rises at W and Y, sinks at X and Z
(c) from X towards W (high to low, towards the equator)
(d) deflected to the right into a curved path
(e) cold, dense air sinks at the pole forming high pressure and flows to the sub-polar low

questions.q: Which bacterium converts some nitrates back into nitrogen gas?
questions.a: Pseudomonas: it is a denitrifying bacterium that converts some nitrates back into nitrogen gas.

questions.q: Which of these is a step in the slow carbon cycle?
o: Dead plants buried for millions of years and changed into coal
A wheat crop taking in CO2 during one growing season
Fallen leaves decomposing in a few months
questions.a: Dead plants buried for millions of years and changed into coal: the slow cycle forms fossil fuels over millions of years, while photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition belong to the fast cycle.

questions.q: (a) What is a biogeochemical cycle? (b) Name two nutrients that are recycled by such cycles.
questions.a: (a) The cyclic movement of matter and energy between the abiotic (non-living) and biotic (living) components of the Earth. (b) Any two of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen.
s: (a) cyclic movement of matter and energy between abiotic and biotic components
(b) two of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen

questions.q: (a) Name two processes that use up oxygen from the atmosphere and release CO2. (b) Name the process that restores oxygen. (c) What three things does this process use?
questions.a: (a) Respiration and combustion of fuels. (b) Photosynthesis. (c) Sunlight, water and CO2.
s: (a) respiration and combustion
(b) photosynthesis
(c) sunlight, water and CO2

questions.q: The events below happen in and around a field of pea plants (a legume). For each, name the process of the nitrogen cycle and the bacterium or organisms that carry it out. (a) Nitrogen gas from the air is changed into ammonia in the root nodules of the pea plants. (b) Ammonia in the soil is changed into nitrite. (c) Nitrite is changed into nitrate. (d) A goat that ate the pea plants dies, and its body is broken down, returning ammonia to the soil. (e) Some nitrate in the soil is changed back into nitrogen gas.
questions.a: (a) Nitrogen fixation, by Rhizobium. (b) Nitrification, by Nitrosomonas. (c) Nitrification, by Nitrobacter. (d) Ammonification, by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi. (e) Denitrification, by Pseudomonas.
s: (a) nitrogen fixation, Rhizobium
(b) nitrification, Nitrosomonas
(c) nitrification, Nitrobacter
(d) ammonification, decomposers (bacteria and fungi)
(e) denitrification, Pseudomonas

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the carbon cycle.
I. Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition belong to the fast cycle, which works over days to years.
II. When fossil fuels are burnt, carbon stored over millions of years is released as CO2 on a very short time scale.
III. Ocean water absorbs CO2 to form carbonate and bicarbonate ions, which phytoplankton use for photosynthesis.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III: all three are correct. The fast cycle works over days to years, burning releases the carbon of fossil fuels quickly, and phytoplankton use the carbonate and bicarbonate ions formed when the ocean absorbs CO2.

questions.q: True or False: 'Global warming makes the atmosphere hold less moisture, so it will only bring droughts.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, causing heavier rains in some areas (like intensified monsoons) and droughts elsewhere.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, giving heavier rains in some areas and droughts in others

questions.q: Meera says, 'The carbon in coal has nothing to do with the CO2 that plants take in, so burning coal cannot upset the carbon cycle.' Is she right? Explain in three steps.
questions.a: No. (1) Coal formed from dead plants that were buried and changed over millions of years in the slow cycle; those plants had taken carbon from atmospheric CO2 by photosynthesis. (2) Burning coal releases this stored carbon back as CO2 on a very short time scale. (3) Carbon locked away over millions of years is returned within a few years, so atmospheric CO2 rises (as the Keeling curve shows), intensifying the greenhouse effect and upsetting the balance of the cycle.
s: coal came from buried plants that once took in atmospheric CO2
burning releases that carbon as CO2 on a very short time scale
so CO2 builds up faster than it was stored, upsetting the balance: Meera is wrong

questions.q: What is the process called in which excess nitrates from fertilisers cause algal blooms in rivers and lakes that deplete oxygen and kill fish?
questions.a: Eutrophication: excess nitrogen from overused fertilisers causes algal blooms that deplete oxygen and kill fish.

questions.q: How is the harmful ozone near the ground in cities formed?
o: Ozone falls down from the stratosphere at night
CFCs from refrigerators react with soil
questions.a: Vehicular emissions react with sunlight to form ground-level smog and ground-level ozone, which is harmful for health.

questions.q: (a) Name the global agreement that started the recovery of the ozone layer. (b) Name the two agreements on reducing CO2 emissions that the chapter says have been less successful.
questions.a: (a) The Montreal Protocol. (b) The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
s: (a) Montreal Protocol
(b) Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement

questions.q: A reef survey team finds coral reefs and plankton under stress in a region where atmospheric CO2 has been rising for decades. Which chain from the chapter explains this?
o: More CO2 is absorbed by the ocean, the sea water becomes more acidic, and this threatens plankton and coral reefs
More CO2 makes the ocean colder, so plankton and corals freeze
More CO2 thickens the ozone layer, so less sunlight reaches the reefs
More CO2 adds nitrates to the sea, so algal blooms cover the reefs
questions.a: Excess atmospheric CO2 increases absorption by the ocean, making sea water more acidic, which threatens tiny plankton and coral reefs and disrupts marine ecosystems.

questions.q: A large forest on a hill slope is cleared. Name three different effects of this clearing given in the chapter, and for each name a sphere of the Earth that it affects.
questions.a: Any three, each with a reasonable sphere: less photosynthesis and transpiration, which can lower the local rainfall (atmosphere or hydrosphere); a change in the surface albedo (atmosphere or geosphere); more soil erosion without tree roots to hold the soil (geosphere); habitat loss and a decline in biodiversity as species lose their homes (biosphere). Accept any reasonable sphere with a correct effect.
s: first effect from the chapter with a reasonable sphere
second effect from the chapter with a reasonable sphere
third effect from the chapter with a reasonable sphere

questions.q: At a school debate on climate, Rohit argues, 'Forests and oceans soak up carbon dioxide, so however much coal and oil we burn, nature will take up the extra and nothing will change.' (a) Name the two natural carbon sinks the chapter mentions. (b) What does the chapter say burning fossil fuels and deforestation do to these sinks? (c) Explain how clearing a forest weakens it as a sink. (d) Decide whether Rohit is right, and name one action from the chapter that would help.
questions.a: (a) Forests and oceans. (b) Burning fossil fuels and deforestation saturate these natural carbon sinks, so the excess CO2 stays in the air and intensifies greenhouse warming, disrupting the carbon cycle. (c) Clearing forests decreases photosynthesis, so less CO2 is taken out of the air by the trees. (d) Rohit is wrong: the sinks can be saturated, and atmospheric CO2 has kept rising. Helpful actions include switching to renewable energy such as solar and wind, conserving energy or planting trees.
s: (a) forests and oceans
(b) they saturate the sinks, so excess CO2 intensifies greenhouse warming
(c) less photosynthesis, so less CO2 is taken up
(d) Rohit is wrong, with one action such as renewable energy, conserving energy or planting trees

questions.q: The Haber-Bosch process uses about 1-2% of global energy. In a model, the world uses 1500 units of energy a year, and all its street lights use 20 units. A planner claims, 'If this fertiliser were no longer made, the energy saved would certainly be more than all the street lights use.' (a) Find the range of energy the process uses in the model. (b) Is the claim certainly true? Justify with a calculation.
questions.a: (a) 1% of 1500 = 15 units and 2% of 1500 = 30 units, so between 15 and 30 units. (b) No, it is not certain. The saving is more than 20 units only if the process uses more than 20 / 1500 × 100 ≈ 1.3% of the energy; anywhere between 1% and about 1.3% the saving (15 to 20 units) would be less, so the data does not prove the claim.
s: (a) between 15 and 30 units
(b) not certain: the saving exceeds 20 units only above about 1.3%, so it could be 15-20 units

questions.q: A family in Pune uses 180 units of electricity a month. Inspired by Mission LiFE, they adopt simple habits such as switching off unused lights and fans, which cut their use by 15%. They then fit a rooftop solar system that supplies 60 units a month of what they still need. The chapter says one unit is 3.6 × 10^6 J. (a) Find the units saved by the habits. (b) Find the units they still take from the grid each month. (c) Find the total monthly reduction in grid electricity, in units and in joules. (d) A neighbour says the habits were not worth the effort, because the solar system alone saves more. Using your figures, give one point for and one point against her view.
questions.a: (a) 15% of 180 = 27 units. (b) 180 - 27 = 153 units; 153 - 60 = 93 units from the grid. (c) 27 + 60 = 87 units = 87 × 3.6 × 10^6 J = 3.132 × 10^8 J. (d) For her view: the solar system saves 60 units a month, more than twice the 27 units saved by habits. Against it: the habits cost nothing, and together the two cut 87 units, 27 more than solar alone; the chapter says individuals help by saving energy as well as by switching to renewables.
s: (a) 27 units saved
(b) 93 units still from the grid
(d) for: solar saves 60 units against 27; against: habits are free and add 27 units, total 87
